**Setup.** Let $n = 10$ be the number of lilypads. A failed hop at position $i$ costs $i$ hops: $i-1$ correct hops to reach position $i$, plus the wrong hop. A failure also tells Kelvin that the pad he tried is not the $i$-th pad, so he can rule it out for that position.

**Strategy.** For position $i$, there are $n-i+1$ candidate pads. Kelvin tries them one at a time. Each failure eliminates one candidate, so he needs at most $n-i$ failures before finding the correct pad.

**Worst-case count.** The failures at position $i$ cost at most $i(n-i)$ hops. The final successful traversal takes $n$ correct hops. So the total is

$$
n + \sum_{i=1}^{n} i(n-i).
$$

Using $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i(n-i) = \dfrac{(n-1)n(n+1)}{6}$:

$$
n + \frac{(n-1)n(n+1)}{6}.
$$

For $n = 10$:

$$
10 + \frac{9 \cdot 10 \cdot 11}{6} = 10 + 165 = 175.
$$

**Optimality.** Each wrong hop eliminates only one candidate at one position, and the order is fixed. An adversary can always answer so that Kelvin's failures are maximized, so no strategy beats this worst case. I did not write out a formal adversary proof, but this matches the standard solution to this problem.

ANSWER: 175
